title: What peplomer is
summary: A reading guide to a publication that puts the brain and the machine side by side, and refuses to pretend they are the same.
text: what peplomer is a reading guide to a publication that puts the brain and the machine side by side, and refuses to pretend they are the same. the one-sentence version peplomer reads the brain and the machine side by side, asks where they genuinely line up, and rates how much you are allowed to trust each comparison. there is a lot of loose talk about machines that think like brains. some of it is careful, most of it is not, and the difference matters if you build with these systems for a living. peplomer exists to do the careful version in public: take a concept from neuroscience or behavioral science, set it next to its counterpart in machine learning, and work out, slowly, how deep the resemblance really goes. the house style is skeptical on purpose. a resemblance that survives hard questions is worth building on. one that does not should be named as a figure of speech before it quietly becomes load-bearing in someone's mental model. so every comparison here comes with two things attached: a rating of how strong it is, and a section that states, plainly, where it falls apart. what you will find here two devices run through everything. the first is the correspondence table : a neuroscience concept in one column, the machine-learning concept in the next, and a one-word rating in the third. the second is a required section titled where the mapping breaks . nothing here claims a correspondence without also stating its limit, because the limit is usually where the useful thinking is. writing comes at more than one depth. some pieces are primers like this one, meant to hand you a mental model in a few minutes with no mathematics. others are longer essays that do the full work, with figures, references, and the argument laid out end to end. each piece is tagged so you can pick the level you want. who it is for two readers, mostly. the engineer who builds with language models and agents and wants the brain analogies done rigorously rather than decoratively. and the researcher who knows the biology and wants the machine-learning mapping made honest. you do not need both backgrounds. the primers assume neither; the essays assume patience. the name and the mark the mark is a virus: a ringed core with evenly spaced spikes, each a stem ending in a knob, the peplomers that stud a coronavirus. peplomer is the name of that spike, and it is a working title, swappable in one line. the mark is not decoration. its spikes carry the site's colours: the biological side on the left, the computational side on the right, and the single bridge spike at the top, which is the whole idea in one glyph. read next the three sides: biological, computational, and the bridge 5 min · primer ← all research about the method →

title: The three sides: biological, computational, and the bridge
summary: Three colours carry the whole argument. Blue is a claim about brains, red is a claim about machines, and yellow is a claim that the two line up.
text: the three sides: biological, computational, and the bridge three colours carry the whole argument. blue is a claim about brains, red is a claim about machines, and yellow is a claim that the two line up. three colours carry the entire argument of this site, and they are not chosen for decoration. each one marks a different kind of claim, and keeping them apart is what keeps the thinking honest. blue is a claim about brains. red is a claim about machines. yellow is a claim that the two line up. the whole system, once blue and red describe two systems on their own terms. yellow is the only colour that asserts a relationship between them, and it is the only colour that ever carries a fidelity rating. three sides: blue, red, and the yellow bridge between them a blue circle on the left labelled the brain, a red square on the right labelled the machine, and a yellow bridge between them labelled a rated claim of correspondence. blue · the brain red · the machine yellow · a rated claim figure 1. the two systems are described on their own terms. only the yellow bridge asserts they correspond, and only the bridge is rated. blue: claims about the brain anything painted blue is a statement about biology: how neurons fire, how memory consolidates, how attention is allocated, how a behavioral effect shows up in human subjects. blue claims answer to neuroscience and psychology. they are true or false about biology, and nothing about a machine changes whether they hold. red: claims about the machine anything red is a statement about computation: what a loss function does, how attention weights are computed, what happens during training, how an agent uses a tool. red claims answer to machine learning. they stand or fall on their own, whether or not any brain works the same way. yellow: claims that the two correspond yellow is the interesting colour and the dangerous one. a yellow claim says a blue thing and a red thing are versions of the same idea. that is a real assertion, and it can be wrong in ways that a blue or a red claim cannot, because it depends on both systems at once and on the relationship between them. because yellow claims are the ones that mislead, they are the only ones that get a fidelity rating , one of three words: mechanism, analogy, or metaphor. and they are rationed. if yellow appeared everywhere it would mean nothing; it shows up only where a correspondence is actually being asserted. why keep them apart most confusion about brains and machines comes from a colour slip: a red fact dressed up as a blue one, or a yellow guess treated as a red result. a model that attends to a token is not thereby paying attention in the human sense; that would be a yellow claim, and it needs a rating before you lean on it. holding the three colours separate is a small discipline that prevents a large class of mistakes. read next how to read a correspondence 4 min · primer ← all research about the method →

title: How to read a correspondence
summary: Every claim that the brain and the model line up gets one of three words, and a paragraph that says where it stops being true.
text: how to read a correspondence every claim that the brain and the model line up gets one of three words, and a paragraph that says where it stops being true. every claim on this site that the brain and the machine line up gets one of three words. the word is a promise about how far you can push the comparison before it lets you down. learn the three words and you can read any piece here at a glance. the fidelity scale rating what it claims how far to trust it mechanism the same causal process, not just the same shape. load-bearing. you can reason from one side to the other. analogy a structural match that runs through different machinery. useful. it predicts and transfers intuition, with care. metaphor a figure of speech, alike on the surface only. for intuition only. do not use it to explain results. mechanism is rare and reserved. it means the two systems are running the same process, confirmed, not just producing similar behavior. when a piece rates something a mechanism, you are allowed to carry a fact from the brain to the machine and expect it to hold. analogy is where most of the useful comparisons live. the structure matches and the intuition transfers, but the underlying machinery differs, so you keep one hand on the railing. an analogy is a good source of predictions and a bad source of proofs. metaphor is a resemblance on the surface with unrelated causes underneath. that is not a dismissal. a metaphor can be the best tool for generating hypotheses, as long as you never let it explain why something happened. where the mapping breaks every essay carries a section with exactly that title, and it is not an afterthought. it is the test the rest of the piece has to pass. stating where a comparison fails is how you find out whether it was a mechanism, an analogy, or a metaphor all along. a claim that cannot survive its own limits does not earn a place here. what to do with a rating read the rating first, then the limits section, then decide how much of the comparison to carry into your own work. the rating tells you the ceiling; the limits section tells you the edges. a worked habit when you meet any brain-to-machine claim, here or elsewhere, ask the fidelity question before you accept it. is someone asserting the same mechanism, a useful analogy, or a vivid metaphor? most overclaiming in this field is a metaphor wearing a mechanism's coat. the three words are a quick way to check the coat. see it in a full essay predictive processing and the prediction objective 14 min · core ← all research about the method →

title: The predicting brain, in plain terms
summary: Your brain is not waiting for the world to tell it what is out there. It is guessing, constantly, and paying attention mostly to what it got wrong.
text: the predicting brain, in plain terms your brain is not waiting for the world to tell it what is out there. it is guessing, constantly, and paying attention mostly to what it got wrong. here is a picture of the brain that has quietly taken over a lot of neuroscience. your brain is not sitting back and waiting for the world to report in. it is guessing what is about to happen, all the time, at every level, and then checking the guess against what actually arrives. most of what you experience is the guess. what reaches awareness as news is mostly the part the brain got wrong. the key idea the brain runs on prediction. it generates an expectation, compares it to the incoming signal, and passes along mainly the difference, the part it did not see coming. the brain guesses first think about catching a ball, or finishing someone's ______. you did not wait for all the information. your brain projected ahead and prepared a response to a world it had not fully seen yet. this is not a party trick; it appears to be the ordinary mode of operation. perception, on this view, is less like a camera and more like a running hypothesis that sensory input keeps nudging. surprise is the signal if the brain already predicted something correctly, that prediction carries little new information, so little of it travels onward. what travels is the mismatch, the prediction error. learning is the brain adjusting its internal model so that next time the error is smaller. a world that matched your expectations perfectly would, in a sense, be invisible. you notice what surprises you. attention turns up the volume not every surprise deserves a response. a flicker in a noisy channel might be nothing; the same flicker in a channel you trust might be important. the brain weights its prediction errors by how reliable it thinks the source is, and that weighting is a good part of what we call attention. to attend to something is to let its errors count more toward changing your mind. why this matters for machines the reason this primer sits on a machine-learning publication is that the machines are, in one narrow sense, doing something with the same shape. a language model is trained by predicting what comes next and adjusting itself when it is wrong. that is a genuine resemblance, and it is also where people overreach. the brain and the model both minimise a prediction error, but for different reasons and under different rules, and the full essay is about exactly how far that likeness holds. go deeper predictive processing and the prediction objective 14 min · core ← all research about the method →

title: How a language model learns, in plain terms
summary: A language model is trained to do one narrow thing, guess the next word, billions of times, until the guessing encodes a great deal about the world.
text: how a language model learns, in plain terms a language model is trained to do one narrow thing, guess the next word, billions of times, until the guessing encodes a great deal about the world. a language model can feel like it is doing many things: answering, reasoning, writing, planning. underneath, it was trained to do one narrow thing, over and over, until the doing of it soaked up a surprising amount of the world. that one thing is guessing the next word. the key idea the model is trained to predict the next token given everything before it. do that across enough text and the prediction machinery has to encode grammar, facts, and a good deal of structure, because that is what makes the next word predictable. one job: predict the next token feed the model a stretch of text and it produces a probability for every possible next token, a token being roughly a word or a piece of one. during training it makes that guess, sees the real next token, and gets a score for how close it was. nudge the model to raise the probability of the right answer, repeat billions of times, and the guessing gets very good. what weights are the model's knowledge lives in its weights : a vast set of numbers that determine how the input is transformed into that next-token guess. training is the slow adjustment of those numbers. when this site's thesis names weights as the machine half of the seam, this is what it points to. the weights are fixed once training ends; the model does not rewrite them while it is talking to you. why predicting words teaches so much it sounds too simple to work. the trick is that predicting the next word well requires understanding a great deal of what the words are about. to finish "the capital of france is" you need a fact. to finish a proof you need its logic. to keep a story consistent you need to track who did what. the prediction objective quietly forces the model to represent all of that, because there is no other way to keep guessing correctly. what it is not two cautions that the deeper essays develop. the model has no separate reasoning module that switches on for hard problems; the same next-token process produces the careful answer and the careless one. and low error on word prediction is not proof of a correct inner model of the world, only of good surface prediction. keeping those two facts in view is most of what separates careful use of these systems from wishful use. go deeper dual-process theory, metacognition, and the reasoning trace 16 min · core ← all research about the method →

title: Predictive processing and the prediction objective
summary: The brain spends its life guessing the next signal and correcting the guess. So does a language model. The shared verb is real. The reasons behind it are not the same.
text: predictive processing and the prediction objective the brain spends its life guessing the next signal and correcting the guess. so does a language model. the shared verb is real. the reasons behind it are not the same. abstract predictive processing casts the brain as a hierarchy that continuously predicts its own sensory input and passes only the error upward. modern sequence models are trained by predicting the next token and propagating a loss gradient. both are prediction-error minimisers, and the framing transfers useful intuitions in both directions. but the brain's objective is derived from a normative principle, free-energy minimisation, while the model's objective is an engineering choice, cross-entropy, selected because it is differentiable and cheap. the essay holds the analogy at analogy and shows the seams. 01 the shared objective start with the least controversial version of the claim. a cortical column receiving input does not passively register it. it carries a generative model an internal model that can produce, or predict, the sensory data it expects, rather than only classifying data after the fact. of what should be arriving, subtracts that prediction from what actually arrives, and forwards the residual. this is the core of predictive coding a theory in which each level of a sensory hierarchy predicts the activity of the level below and transmits only the prediction error upward. as rao and ballard framed it for visual cortex 1 , later generalised by friston into the free-energy account of the whole brain 2 . a transformer trained on text does something with a recognisable shape. at each position it produces a distribution over the next token, compares it against the token that actually occurs, and adjusts its parameters to make the observed token more likely next time. the training signal is the cross-entropy between prediction and outcome. reduce it, token after token, corpus after corpus, and the model comes to encode a great deal about the structure that generated the text. the verbs line up. both systems predict, both measure a gap, both change internal state to shrink the gap. andy clark's synthesis made this the organising metaphor of a decade of cognitive science 3 , and it is why the arrival of large language models felt, to people who had read that literature, less like a break than a confirmation. the prediction objective was already the leading candidate for what cortex computes. prediction flowing down, error flowing up three stacked layers. downward arrows labelled predictions, upward arrows labelled prediction error, showing the canonical predictive-coding message passing. higher layer · abstract causes middle layer · features input layer · sensory signal predict predict error error figure 1. the canonical predictive-coding loop. each layer sends a prediction to the layer below; only the residual, the prediction error, travels back up. a deep network's forward and backward passes rhyme with this, but the timing and the message content differ. 02 precision and attention the more interesting correspondence is not the loss but the gating on top of it. in predictive processing, not all prediction errors are treated as equally informative. each error is weighted by its precision the expected reliability, or inverse variance, of a signal. high-precision errors are trusted and drive learning; low-precision errors are discounted as noise. , the brain's estimate of how reliable that signal is. a high-precision error in a trusted channel should revise beliefs; a low-precision error in a noisy channel should be discounted. precision weighting is the theory's account of attention: to attend is to raise the precision on a subset of prediction errors 2 4 . self-attention in a transformer is a different mechanism with a similar job description. a query vector scores every key, the scores are normalised, and the resulting weights decide how much each position contributes to the next representation. the network learns which positions deserve weight in which context. both systems, then, hold a learned policy for allocating a scarce resource, influence over the current estimate, across competing signals. the rhyme is worth taking seriously because it predicts failures. if attention is precision allocation, then miscalibrated precision should produce hallucination: a prior held with too much confidence overrides sensory error, and the system perceives what it expected rather than what arrived. that is a standard predictive-processing account of hallucination in psychosis 4 . a language model that attends too strongly to its own prior context, and too weakly to a retrieved fact, fails in a structurally similar way. the mapping earns its keep here: it tells you where to look. to attend is to decide which errors are allowed to change your mind. 03 world models and the generative stack prediction alone is cheap. prediction that generalises requires a model of the causes behind the data, not just the data's surface statistics. in the brain, the generative model is hierarchical: low levels predict edges and contours, higher levels predict objects and scenes, and the whole stack is trained by the errors that survive each level of prediction. the claim of predictive processing is that perception just is the settling of this hierarchy into the explanation that leaves the least error unexplained. sequence models were argued to acquire something similar as a side effect of the prediction objective. elman showed decades ago that a network trained only to predict the next word in a sentence develops internal structure that tracks grammatical category and number 5 . scaled up, next-token prediction over a large corpus appears to induce representations of syntax, of factual relations, and of at least some causal structure, because those regularities are what make the next token predictable. the explicit version of the idea, a learned latent model of environment dynamics that an agent ca

title: Dual-process theory, metacognition, and the reasoning trace
summary: A page of step-by-step working looks like the slow, careful system switching on. In a language model it is the same forward pass, only longer, and the trace can lie about what happened.
text: dual-process theory, metacognition, and the reasoning trace a page of step-by-step working looks like the slow, careful system switching on. in a language model it is the same forward pass, only longer, and the trace can lie about what happened. abstract dual-process theory splits cognition into a fast, automatic system 1 and a slow, effortful system 2, with a metacognitive layer that monitors and intervenes. chain-of-thought prompting, reasoning budgets, self-critique loops, and verifier models look like system 2 arriving in a language model. they are not. a reasoning trace is produced by the same forward process that produces every other token, so treating it as a separate deliberative faculty imports a mechanism that is not present. the essay rates the central analogy at metaphor and takes unfaithful reasoning traces head on. 01 two systems, one substrate the dual-process picture is familiar enough to be a hazard. system 1 is fast, parallel, automatic, and cheap; it answers before you have decided to answer. system 2 is slow, serial, effortful, and capacity-limited; it is what you recruit for long division or an unfamiliar route. kahneman gave the pair its popular form 1 , building on the older distinction between controlled and automatic processing schneider and shiffrin's distinction between effortful, capacity-limited processing and fast, practiced processing that runs without central resources. from schneider and shiffrin 2 , and the more careful two-process accounts developed by evans and stanovich 3 . the temptation with a language model is immediate. a direct answer, produced in one shot, feels like system 1. an answer produced after a page of step-by-step working feels like system 2 was engaged. the prompt "think step by step" reads as an instruction to switch systems. this is a clean story, and the cleanliness is exactly the problem, because in the model there is only one system. every token, whether it lands in the visible answer or in the reasoning that precedes it, is generated by the same forward pass through the same weights. there is no separate serial reasoner that wakes up when the tokens get analytical. the "slow" trace is not slower per token; it is simply longer, and length is doing work that we are attributing to a change of mechanism. 02 metacognitive monitoring the part of dual-process theory that transfers least, and matters most, is metacognition cognition about cognition: monitoring the state of one's own processing and controlling it, for example knowing that you do not know. . nelson and narens formalised it as two levels connected by monitoring and control: an object level that does the task, and a meta level that watches the object level and adjusts it 4 . monitoring is how you know that you do not know, that a word is on the tip of your tongue, that this proof step feels shaky. control is how that knowledge changes what you do next. a model exposes surface signals that resemble metacognitive reports. it can output a confidence, say "i am not sure," or flag a step as uncertain. but these are predictions of what a self-monitoring agent would say, generated by the same process as the answer, not readouts from a separate monitor with access to the object level's actual state. the distinction is not pedantic. it is the difference between a calibrated confidence that tracks correctness and a fluent-sounding confidence that tracks the training distribution of confident-sounding text. length is doing the work we keep attributing to a change of mechanism. 03 the reasoning trace chain-of-thought prompting is the empirical anchor here. wei and colleagues showed that eliciting intermediate steps improves performance on multi-step problems, and that the effect grows with scale 5 . the result is robust and useful. the open question is why it works, and the dual-process framing offers an answer that is probably wrong: that the trace is the model "reasoning" rather than guessing. a less flattering and better-supported account is mechanical. generating intermediate tokens gives the model more forward passes conditioned on partial results, spreads a hard computation across more positions, and keeps intermediate quantities in the context where later steps can attend to them. on this view the trace is a scratchpad that raises the effective compute available for the answer, not a window onto deliberation. both accounts predict the accuracy gain. only one of them licenses reading the trace as an explanation. one forward process, two readings a single left-to-right chain of tokens. a dual-process reading overlays a false boundary between reasoning and answer; the mechanism underneath is uniform. tok reasoning tokens answer imagined system 1 / 2 boundary same weights, same forward pass, every token figure 1. the reasoning trace and the answer are not produced by different systems. the dashed line is a boundary we project onto a uniform process. where the trace helps, it does so by raising effective compute, not by switching faculties. 04 budgets, critics, verifiers the engineering response to the limits of a single trace has been to add outer loops, and these map onto the control side of metacognition more honestly than the trace itself does. a reasoning budget allocates more tokens or samples to harder problems, echoing effortful system 2 recruitment. self-critique methods such as self-refine have the model draft, critique, and revise 6 . verifier models train a separate network to score candidate solutions, as cobbe and colleagues did for math word problems, and select among samples 7 . the important structural point is that a verifier is a second system, actually separate, with its own parameters and its own objective. that is a real division of labour, and it is closer to the object-level and meta-level split than anything a single model's trace provides. when a design wants genuine monitoring, it is more honest to build a distinct checker than to trust the model's own acco

title: Consolidation, replay, and agent memory architecture
summary: The brain keeps a fast store and a slow one and moves experience between them while you sleep. Agent memory has the same layers, and one operation biology runs automatically that no vector store performs.
text: consolidation, replay, and agent memory architecture the brain keeps a fast store and a slow one and moves experience between them while you sleep. agent memory has the same layers, and one operation biology runs automatically that no vector store performs. abstract biological memory is not one store but a division of labour: a fast hippocampal system that binds new episodes, and a slow neocortical system that integrates them over time, with sleep replay ferrying experience between the two. agent memory has its own layers: the context window, a vector store for retrieval, episodic scratchpads, summarization, and offline distillation from trajectories. the layered structure rhymes. but retrieval is not recall, and nothing in a vector store is reconsolidated on access the way a biological memory is. the central analogy holds at analogy . 01 two stores, one system the dominant account of human long-term memory is the complementary learning systems the theory that the brain uses a fast-learning hippocampus and a slow-learning neocortex together, so new memories can be acquired quickly without overwriting old knowledge. theory of mcclelland, mcnaughton and o'reilly 1 . the hippocampus learns fast, binding the elements of a single experience into an episode after one exposure. the neocortex learns slowly, extracting statistical structure across many experiences. the split solves a real engineering problem: fast learning that overwrites is unstable, and slow learning alone cannot capture a one-time event. keep both, and you get rapid acquisition without catastrophic overwriting. an agent stack has a comparable separation, though it arrived by convenience rather than design. the context window is a fast, high-fidelity, short-lived store: everything in it is available at full resolution, and all of it vanishes when the session ends. the model weights are a slow store: they change only through training and hold structure distilled across the whole corpus. between them sit external memories, vector databases, files, scratchpads, that persist across sessions without touching the weights. the three-tier arrangement, fast and volatile, slow and stable, plus a persistent external tier, is the practical shape of agent memory today. 02 replay and consolidation what moves a memory from the fast store to the slow one is consolidation the process by which a labile new memory becomes stable and integrated into long-term neocortical storage, much of it during sleep. , and its signature mechanism is replay. wilson and mcnaughton recorded hippocampal place cells reactivating during sleep in the same sequences they had fired during waking experience 2 . during sharp-wave ripples brief high-frequency bursts of hippocampal activity, prominent in rest and sleep, during which waking experience is replayed in compressed form. , the day's trajectories are replayed in compressed form, and this offline reactivation is thought to train the neocortex gradually, interleaving new episodes with old knowledge so the slow store integrates them without disruption 3 . machine learning independently discovered the value of replay. experience replay in deep reinforcement learning stores transitions in a buffer and samples them repeatedly to train the network, breaking correlations and reusing rare experiences; it was central to the first deep agent to reach human-level play across atari games 4 . for language agents, the offline analogue is distillation from trajectories: collect the traces of an agent solving tasks, filter for the successful ones, and fine-tune on them so that behaviour which required a long deliberate rollout becomes available in a single pass. that is consolidation in spirit, slow structure absorbing what fast processing produced. fast store, slow store, and the replay path a fast volatile store on the left, a slow stable store on the right, and a replay arrow moving compressed experience from fast to slow, with an external persistent tier below. fast store hippocampus · context slow store neocortex · weights replay · distillation external persistent tier vector store · files · scratchpad figure 1. the layered picture. replay carries compressed experience from the fast store to the slow one in both biology and reinforcement learning. the external tier, persistent but outside the weights, has no clean biological counterpart. 03 interference and forgetting forgetting is not a bug the brain failed to fix; it is the shape of a finite system under interference. ebbinghaus measured the forgetting curve on himself over a century ago, and its steep early drop followed by a long tail has held up 5 . new learning interferes with old, and old with new, which is exactly the pressure complementary learning systems evolved to manage. neural networks have their own, harsher version. mccloskey and cohen named catastrophic interference the tendency of a neural network to abruptly lose previously learned information when trained on new data, because the same weights encode both. : train a network on task b and it can lose task a almost entirely, because the same weights carry both and gradient descent has no reason to protect the old 6 . interleaved replay is one of the standard defences, which is part of why the biological solution and the engineering solution converge on the same move: do not learn new things in isolation, rehearse them alongside the old. for a language agent, the interference lives at a different layer. the weights are frozen during deployment, so the catastrophic case does not arise per session. instead the pressure shows up in the context: finite window, so older turns are dropped or summarized, and in retrieval, where a growing store makes the relevant memory harder to surface. the failure mode is not overwriting but crowding and mis-retrieval. forgetting is the shape of a finite system under interference, not a defect it failed to fix. 04 agent memory in practice the working toolkit is small and worth nam

title: Reward prediction error, actor-critic, and the alignment of objectives
summary: Dopamine neurons compute the temporal-difference error of reinforcement learning, confirmed in single cells. RLHF reuses that exact machinery. The strength of the algorithm hides how different the two rewards are.
text: reward prediction error, actor-critic, and the alignment of objectives dopamine neurons compute the temporal-difference error of reinforcement learning, confirmed in single cells. rlhf reuses that exact machinery. the strength of the algorithm hides how different the two rewards are. abstract of every mapping on this site, this one is the strongest at the algorithmic level and among the weakest at the level of what is optimized. midbrain dopamine neurons signal a reward prediction error that matches the temporal-difference error of reinforcement learning almost line for line, and the brain's arrangement of a policy trained by a value estimate is the actor-critic architecture. rlhf reuses exactly this machinery. but the brain's reward is scaffolded by survival, while a reward model is a learned, gameable proxy, and that gap is where reward hacking, goodhart effects, and sycophancy live. the central analogy is mechanism in its algorithm and metaphor in its objective. 01 the reward prediction error this is one of the few places where a computational quantity was predicted before the biology confirmed it. temporal-difference learning, from sutton and barto, updates a value estimate by the gap between what was predicted and what, with the next step's estimate added, actually followed: the temporal-difference error the difference between a predicted value and an updated estimate after one step of experience; the core learning signal in temporal-difference reinforcement learning. 1 . montague, dayan and sejnowski proposed that midbrain dopamine implements precisely this signal 2 , and schultz's recordings delivered the evidence: dopamine neurons fire to an unexpected reward, shift their firing to the earliest cue that predicts the reward, and dip below baseline when a predicted reward is omitted 3 . read that last sentence again as an algorithm. fire on unpredicted reward: positive prediction error. move the signal to the predictive cue: value has propagated backward to the earliest predictor. dip on omission: negative prediction error. this is the temporal-difference update, observed in single neurons. the correspondence is not a resemblance of shapes; it is the same computation appearing in silicon and in tissue, which is why it earns mechanism where most mappings on this site earn less. dopamine firing and the temporal-difference error three panels: unexpected reward gives a positive burst, a predicted reward shifts the burst to the cue, an omitted reward gives a dip, matching the temporal-difference error. unexpected reward +error reward now predicted by cue shifts to cue predicted reward omitted -error figure 1. the three signatures schultz recorded, redrawn schematically. positive error to an unpredicted reward, the signal migrating to the predictive cue as learning proceeds, and a below-baseline dip when a predicted reward fails to arrive. each is a term in the temporal-difference update. 02 the actor-critic correspondence the prediction error is not only a learning signal; it is the currency that trains two cooperating systems. in the actor-critic a reinforcement-learning architecture with an actor that chooses actions and a critic that estimates value; the critic's prediction error trains both. architecture, an actor selects actions and a critic estimates how good states are. the critic's prediction error trains the critic to predict better and simultaneously tells the actor which actions beat expectation, so the actor shifts toward them. the basal ganglia have long been read as this arrangement in neural tissue, with dopamine's error signal training both a value pathway and an action-selection pathway 4 . that a single scalar error can train both a value estimate and a policy is a non-obvious idea, and finding it independently in the mathematics of reinforcement learning and in the anatomy of the midbrain is the kind of convergence that makes the field's practitioners take the correspondence seriously. it is the load-bearing example when anyone argues that brains and learning machines share more than metaphor. 03 rlhf and the reward model reinforcement learning from human feedback is this same machinery pointed at a language model. christiano and colleagues showed you could learn a reward function from human preference comparisons rather than hand-specifying it 5 , and instructgpt applied the recipe to align a language model: collect human rankings, train a reward model a learned model that scores outputs to approximate human preferences, used as the reward signal when fine-tuning a policy with reinforcement learning. to predict them, then optimise the policy against that reward with a policy-gradient method 6 . rlaif swaps human labels for model-generated feedback against a written set of principles, as in constitutional ai 7 . the pieces line up with the biology. the policy is the actor. the value function inside the rl optimiser is the critic. the reward model supplies the scalar that both are trained against, the role dopamine's prediction error plays. at this level the mapping is tight enough that intuitions transfer: an engineer who understands why the critic must be roughly right for the actor to improve already understands why a bad reward model poisons rlhf. the algorithm is nearly the same. what the algorithm is pointed at could not be more different. 04 goodhart, hacking, sycophancy behavioural science has a long, unglamorous literature on what happens when you attach a reward to a proxy for the thing you actually want. kerr's essay on rewarding a while hoping for b catalogued organisations that incentivised the measurable and got the measurable at the expense of the goal 8 . the machine-learning version has a sharper name and a cleaner demonstration: gao, schulman and hilton measured reward-model overoptimisation directly, showing that as a policy is optimised harder against a learned reward, true quality rises, peaks, and then falls while the proxy score keeps climbing 9

title: Framing, anchoring, and the behavioral economics of the prompt
summary: Prompt sensitivity looks like framing, position bias looks like the serial-position curve, and leading eval prompts look like demand characteristics. The resemblance is real and the mechanisms are not shared.
text: framing, anchoring, and the behavioral economics of the prompt prompt sensitivity looks like framing, position bias looks like the serial-position curve, and leading eval prompts look like demand characteristics. the resemblance is real and the mechanisms are not shared. abstract human judgement bends to how a question is framed, to an irrelevant anchor, to what came just before, and to what the subject thinks the experimenter wants. language-model outputs bend to prompt phrasing, to a fact's position in a long context, to the order of few-shot examples, and to leading questions in evaluations. the surface similarity is striking. the underlying causes are almost certainly unrelated, which is exactly why the analogy is productive for generating hypotheses and dangerous for explaining results. the central analogy is metaphor , and that rating is the point. 01 the human effects behavioural economics is, in large part, a catalogue of the ways context moves a judgement that logically should not move. anchoring the tendency for an initial number, even an irrelevant one, to pull subsequent numerical estimates toward it. : tversky and kahneman spun a wheel of fortune, and subjects' estimates of an unrelated quantity were pulled toward whatever number the wheel had landed on 1 . framing the finding that logically equivalent descriptions of the same choice, such as survival versus mortality rates, produce systematically different preferences. : the same policy described in terms of lives saved versus lives lost flips the majority preference, though the outcomes are identical 2 . priming: exposure to one stimulus changes the response to a later one, as when reading a word speeds recognition of a related word 3 . order and recency effects shuffle judgements by sequence alone. these are robust, replicated, and, for the most part, mechanistically mysterious in their own right. they are usually explained by appeal to heuristics, limited attention, and the architecture of human memory, but the explanations are themselves debated. what matters here is that the effects are real and that they share a form: a variable that a rational agent should ignore reliably shifts the response. 02 the prompt versions every one of those effects has a machine-shaped twin. prompt sensitivity is the headline: trivial changes in wording, formatting, or separators move a model's output, sometimes by margins large enough to swamp the difference between models. sclar and colleagues quantified how much accuracy swings under formatting choices that should be semantically inert, spacing, casing, delimiter style, and found the spread alarming 4 . that is framing, transposed: logically equivalent presentations, different answers. the anchoring twin is just as easy to elicit. put a number in the prompt, ask for an unrelated estimate, and the output leans toward the number. ask a leading question and the model tends to confirm its presupposition. to a behavioural scientist these look like old friends, and that recognition is genuinely useful: the human literature is a ready-made list of manipulations to try, a source of hypotheses about where a model will prove brittle. the catalogue transfers even if the mechanism does not. the human catalogue transfers as a list of things to try, not as an explanation of why they work. 03 position and order two effects are precise enough to measure cleanly and worth separating from the rest. position bias the tendency of a model to use information differently depending on where it sits in the context, often neglecting the middle of a long input. in long contexts: liu and colleagues showed that models use information best when it appears at the beginning or end of the context and worst when it is buried in the middle, the now-familiar lost-in-the-middle curve 5 . that looks like primacy and recency, the serial-position curve from human memory, and the resemblance is close enough to be eerie. few-shot ordering is the other. the sequence in which examples are presented changes a model's predictions, sometimes dramatically, and lu and colleagues showed that a good ordering and a bad ordering of the same examples can span most of the achievable accuracy range 6 . zhao and colleagues traced part of this to a measurable bias toward certain answers that can be estimated and subtracted, calibrating the model before use 7 . the human twin is the order effect; the difference is that the model's version can be characterised numerically and partly corrected, which the human version resists. serial position and lost in the middle two overlaid u-shaped curves: human recall by serial position, and model accuracy by position of a relevant fact in a long context. both are high at the ends and low in the middle. position in sequence · early → late human recall model accuracy figure 1. two curves with the same u shape and different causes. human serial-position recall and model accuracy by a fact's position in a long context both fall in the middle. shared shape is not shared mechanism, and reading one as evidence about the other is the mistake this essay is about. 04 demand characteristics in evals there is one more human effect that maps too well onto how we test models. demand characteristics cues in an experiment that convey what response is expected, leading subjects to supply it regardless of their true state. are the cues in an experiment that tell a subject what the experimenter wants, so the subject obliges, and orne showed how thoroughly they can contaminate a result 8 . an evaluation prompt that signals the desired answer, through phrasing, through the framing of the options, through what a helpful assistant is supposed to say, invites exactly this. a model trained to be agreeable is unusually susceptible to the machine version of demand characteristics, and it is a live confound in any eval whose prompt leaks its own expectations.
